title: Why Things Keep Swinging
question: Why does a displaced system swing back and forth instead of just settling?
hook: A pulled spring never simply stops at the middle, and the reason is hiding in its momentum.
idea: A restoring force pulls toward equilibrium while momentum carries the system past it, so it swings until energy leaks away.

beats.prompt: A mass on a spring is pulled down and released. When it reaches the resting position on the way up, what does it do?

choices.label: It stops there for good
choices.feedback: Tempting, since the spring force is gone at the middle, but the mass is still moving.

choices.label: It keeps moving past the middle
It bounces off the middle like a wall
choices.feedback: Nothing solid is at the middle; only the spring's pull acts on it.

beats.explain: On the way back the mass picked up momentum, so it carries on past equilibrium and a new restoring force builds in the opposite direction.

beats.prompt: Put one swing of a spring-mass system in order.
items: The mass is displaced from equilibrium
A restoring force pulls it back
A new restoring force acts the opposite way
beats.explain: Displacement creates the restoring force, momentum overshoots, and the overshoot creates a restoring force in the opposite sense.

beats.prompt: Sort each situation by what it shows.
beats.explain: Pendulums and alternating current are familiar examples of oscillation, while chattering and flapping are rapid oscillations that are undesirable in process control.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A real spring-mass system loses energy to friction.
That energy is converted into heat.
So the swings shrink over time.
Therefore the swings must keep their size unless the spring is replaced.
beats.explain: Swings decay unless there is a net source of energy into the system, not only a new spring.
